In one minute

Do we need to do anything? No. Keep the regular monthly investing going.

What's the economic weather? The US economy is in the expansion phase: growing faster than normal, and speeding up. No warning signs of a US recession right now.

Anything worth a look? Long-term themes steadily gaining on world shares: AI and computer chips. That is the one reading that has helped a little in past tests. Running hot, so don't chase: Cyber security and Health and ageing. Japan is gaining on world shares, but for regions that has not been a good sign in past tests.

How much to trust this? Use it to notice things, not to decide. The economic phase is background, not a timing tool. The theme readings are tested below and are recorded weekly so we can check them.

The economic weather

The US economy is in the Expansion phase: growing faster than normal, and speeding up. It has been for 9 months.

Recoverybelow normal, improving
Expansionabove normal, improving
Contractionbelow normal, worsening
Slowdownabove normal, worsening

The leading indicator, last 5 years

A mix of signals that usually turn before the economy does. Above the dashed line the economy is growing faster than normal; the slope says whether it is speeding up or slowing. Latest: 101.0 for 2026-09.

What has happened in this phase before

Since 1999, in the expansion phase, US shares went up over the next three months 80% of the time (average +3.2%).

Did better than the market: tech companies (+1.9%), energy companies (+0.7%), healthcare companies (+0.7%).

Did worse: long-term US government bonds (-2.4%), gold (-2.1%), everyday-goods companies (food, household) (-1.7%).

Figures are the average over the next three months compared with the S&P 500. Only 10 separate spells of this phase since 1999, and the OECD tidies up its past figures, so the history looks cleaner than it felt at the time. Treat it as a tilt, not a rule.

All four phases

Recession warning lights

No warning signs of a US recession right now.

Interest-rate curvenormal (long-term borrowing costs more than short-term)

When it costs more to borrow for 3 months than for 10 years, lenders expect hard times. It has turned upside down before every US recession since 1968, usually 6 to 18 months ahead.

10-year minus 3-month US borrowing cost, in percentage points. Below the red line = upside down.

Now: +0.87% (2026-10-28). Rule: Red if below 0; amber if under 0.5 or upside down in the last year.

Unemployment risingsteady

When the US jobless rate rises half a point above its low of the past year, a recession has almost always already begun.

How far US unemployment is above its low of the past year, in points.

Now: 0.00 points (2026-09-01). Rule: Red at 0.5 or more; amber at 0.3.

New jobless claims0% above the year's low

The earliest sign of layoffs. It shows up weeks before the unemployment rate does.

Weekly jobless claims (4-week average), % above their low of the past year.

Now: 198k a week (2026-10-17). Rule: Red if the 4-week average is 20% above the year's low; amber at 10%.

Company borrowing costsfalling (-0.20 points on a year ago)

When lenders get nervous they charge companies more. Rising fast usually means lenders see defaults coming.

Change over a year in the extra interest riskier US companies pay, in points.

Now: 1.45% extra (2026-10-26). Rule: Red if up 0.75 points in a year; amber if up 0.35.

How easy money is to geteasier than normal

Combines 105 measures of lending, borrowing and market stress. Above zero means money is harder to get than usual.

Chicago Fed index of how easy money is to get. Above the red line = tighter than normal.

Now: -0.49 (2026-10-23). Rule: Red above 0; amber above -0.2.

Ahead of world shares over both the past year and the last three months, but not by an unusual amount. Its price is above its average of the last 40 weeks.

A steady trend. Fine to keep adding slowly.

This reading has helped a little in the past: over the next six months, themes reading "Building" did 3.6% better than world shares on average and beat them 59% of the time.

Our sources are talking about it more: about 2.6 times as often as usual.

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: Every AI model is trained and run on specialist chips, and the big tech firms are spending hundreds of billions a year on them. A handful of companies make almost all of them.

What could go wrong: The spending is a boom: if AI doesn't pay its way, orders get cut fast and chip shares fall hard.

Way in: SMGB: about 25 of the biggest chip companies (Nvidia, TSMC, ASML). Yearly fee 0.35%. VanEck Semiconductor UCITS ETF, ID IE00BMC38736

Or SEMI: a wider basket of chip companies worldwide. Yearly fee 0.35%. iShares MSCI Global Semiconductors UCITS ETF USD (Acc), ID IE000I8KRLL9

Measured with the US fund SOXX, which has a longer price history.

What could go wrong: The shares are often priced for fast growth, so a slowdown hits them hard.

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: Central banks have been buying gold at record pace to rely less on the dollar, and gold tends to hold its value when governments borrow heavily or inflation stays high.

What could go wrong: Gold pays no income, and it can go nowhere for years once the fear fades.

Way in: SGLN: real gold bars held in a vault. Yearly fee 0.12%. iShares Physical Gold ETC, ID IE00B4ND3602

Regions and company size

Parts of the world market rather than stories. World shares are about two-thirds American, so a region "beating world shares" mostly means it is catching up with the US. Same labels and charts as the themes, tested separately. Pick a period to redraw every chart:

What the past says: over the years tested, regions beat world shares over the next six months only 39% of the time, whatever their label, because the US kept pulling ahead. No label picked the winners. The least bad was "Out of favour" (43%); regions that had been doing well did worst afterwards. Use this section to see where the world is moving, not as a reason to switch.

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: Japan's stock exchange is pushing companies to pay shareholders and use their large cash piles better, and inflation has returned after 30 years. Both help shares if they last.

What could go wrong: Japan's money is tied to its central bank: a sudden rise in the yen or in its interest rates has hit shares hard before.

Way in: SJPA: about 1,000 Japanese companies of all sizes. Yearly fee 0.12%. iShares Core MSCI Japan IMI UCITS ETF, ID IE00B4L5YX21

Measured with the US fund EWJ, which has a longer price history.

Why it could run for years: The least-watched corner of the market, where good companies can be overlooked before they grow.

What could go wrong: Swings much harder than anything else here, and many of these companies never make a profit.

Way in: No fund we can buy: justETF lists no fund of tiny companies that reinvests dividends and can be held in an ISA (checked 27 Oct 2026). Shown so we can watch it; the nearest we can buy is the smaller US companies fund above.

Measured with the US fund IWC, which has a longer price history.

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: Over very long periods smaller companies have often beaten big ones (though not in the last 15 years), and they gain most when interest rates fall because they borrow more.

What could go wrong: Many don't make a profit, so they suffer most when rates stay high or the economy slows.

Way in: R2SC: smaller US companies. Yearly fee 0.30%. SPDR Russell 2000 US Small Cap UCITS ETF (Acc), ID IE00BJ38QD84

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: Sits next to the fastest-growing part of the world, with Korea's chip makers and Australia's miners and banks.

What could go wrong: Tied to China's economy through trade, and to the price of the metals Australia digs up.

Way in: VDPG: companies in Australia, South Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand. Yearly fee 0.15%. Vanguard FTSE Developed Asia Pacific ex Japan UCITS ETF (USD) Accumulating, ID IE00BK5BQZ41

The story, the risk, and how to buy it

Why it could run for years: European shares are much cheaper than American ones for each pound of profit, and Europe is now spending heavily on defence, energy and its own industry. Cheap markets can catch up for years.

What could go wrong: They have been cheap for over a decade for a reason: slow growth and few big tech companies. Cheap can stay cheap.

Way in: SMEA: about 400 large and mid-sized European companies, UK included. Yearly fee 0.12%. iShares Core MSCI Europe UCITS ETF EUR (Acc), ID IE00B4K48X80

This week's knock-ons

From the radar of 2026-10-29: short-term moves and who they hit.

Do we need to do anything? No.

What's happening? The cost of hiring an oil tanker is now about 3.4 times what it was 3 months ago, a much bigger move than usual. Our sources are also talking a lot about the oil price, refiners' profit on fuel, spending on AI and computer chips, long-term interest rates, the copper price, how easily companies can borrow, expected inflation and the cost of shipping a container, but those prices haven't moved much, so we treat that as chatter for now.

Anything to buy? Nothing urgent. If you want something to read about: IESU (big US oil and gas companies), IUSU (US electricity companies), FGRD (companies building power grids), COPG (copper mining companies) and GDGB (gold mining companies). These fit our rule of only buying funds that reinvest dividends.

How much to trust this? Not much yet. We tested it on 2019 to 2026: its ideas were right 48% of the time. Picking at random was right 51% of the time. So use it to notice things, not to decide what to buy. It keeps score of every idea, so we will know more in a few months.

A reading only helps if themes with it went on to beat world shares more often than not. Three cautions: most themes only have 10 to 15 years of prices; themes often move together, so the spells overlap; and these ten themes were picked today, knowing which ones became famous, which flatters the past. How the options have done

Every option this page shows is written down the day it first appears, with the price that day, and checked later. "Helped" means it went the way the option implied compared with world shares: an "add" or "keep" helped if it did better, a "don't add", "avoid" or "switch" helped if it did worse. These are options to think about, not advice.
